cards.source_text: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials meet on sidelines - Published President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal. A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech on Tuesday in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race. His comments came on a day of high-level diplomacy. He has been meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda. Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan. He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February. Trump's tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. cards.source_text: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark - Published The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it. Before a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations". Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win". The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory. Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth. His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral". The deal amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US. The new pact says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east. Narsarsuaq is a former civilian airport and World War Two base. It has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were recently surveying, the US North Command confirmed to the BBC. The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit. The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties, This means the US security arrangements are not unfettered and Greenland and Denmark's approval is still needed. Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there. It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland". cards.source_text: Zelensky says Ukraine is ready for an energy ceasefire with Russia On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists that Kyiv is ready to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure if Moscow does the same, with hopes to end the war before winter. "We are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire" if Russia agrees to "not attack our energy system," Zelensky told journalists on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader however said he did not know Moscow's position, expressing hope that the "American side will find a way ... to bring them to any kind of negotiations." cards.source_text: BEIJING, September 23. /TASS/. Chinese President Xi Jinping begins his first state visit to the United States in 11 years on September 23 , with talks with US President Donald Trump expected to focus on stabilizing bilateral ties. The agenda includes fentanyl precursors, mutual moratoriums expiring November 10, rare earth supplies, US tariffs, China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and other high-tech products, and US arms supplies to Taiwan. The sides also agreed to launch an artificial intelligence dialogue to prevent escalation. Trump may seek greater Chinese purchases of US goods, while China is expected to seek lower US tariffs. The sides are discussing tariff reductions covering about $30 billion in goods for each side. The leaders are also expected to discuss the Ukraine crisis, US-Iran tensions, Strait of Hormuz shipping, sanctions, space militarization, US missile systems in Japan and Washington’s Pax Silica technology alliance, as well as "constructive strategic stability." Further talks may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November and G20 summit in December.
cards.source_title: Xi Jinping’s visit to US: what to expect from talks with Trump?

cards.source_text: UNITED NATIONS, September 22. /TASS/. The US presidential administration is studying the possibility of using a law tightening sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil and gas exports, dubbed "hell sanctions" in the media, US leader Donald Trump said while answering reporters' questions ahead of a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. "That's something we're certainly studying. It's a very severe bill," Trump said when asked about the possibility of applying the law. Asked whether he intended to raise the issue of possible secondary sanctions against Russia's trading partners at a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump replied: "Probably." "We're going to talk about a lot. It's going to be a great meeting, and we're going to have a look," he added. On September 18, Trump signed into law legislation passed by the US Congress to tighten sanctions on Russia. The legislation was principally authored by US Senator Lindsey Graham, who died on July 11. It provides for sanctions against Russia's senior political and military leadership and state-owned companies, as well as secondary restrictions against Russia's trading partners. Under the legislation, the United States may impose 100% tariffs on countries that are major purchasers of Russian oil and gas. It also provides for tougher sanctions on Iran.
cards.source_title: US studying tougher Russia sanctions law — Trump

cards.source_text: Viral NATO video falsely framed as ‘war propaganda’ against Russia To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement. One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site. Issued on: A viral NATO video is being falsely framed online as “war propaganda”, with users accusing the Alliance of sharing a “promotional video” designed to prepare the public for imminent war with Russia. But the footage is not new: NATO published it in July 2024 for its 75th anniversary, and it’s been stripped of its original context. The claim comes as European leaders warn of growing Russian hybrid threats, including alleged drone, cyber and sabotage activity. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake. Moscow is facing growing accusations of targeting NATO countries with its hybrid campaign, as a growing number of European leaders have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test the Alliance’s commitment to supporting Ukraine. But amid those tensions, a different claim is spreading online: that NATO is preparing the public for an imminent war with Russia. Pro-Kremlin accounts have been sharing a video they describe as NATO “propaganda” or “promotional material” for a future conflict with Moscow, and some posts have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times, if not millions. The video was also shared by the Russian embassy in the Netherlands, which accused NATO of trying to “inspire the youth to be ready to die for the elites”. It was also amplified in the United States by conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, who made further “white genocide” claims about the video’s portrayal of diversity. However the video is not new footage, and it wasn’t produced to promote an impending war with Russia. The video was created to celebrate the Alliance’s 75th anniversary, and NATO published the video on its official social media accounts in July 2024, ahead of a summit in Washington marking the date. The footage has since been downloaded, stripped of that context and recirculated online as supposed evidence that NATO is preparing the public for war with Russia. Whilst the video is being misinterpreted online, it does not mean tensions between NATO countries and Russia are not intensifying. cards.source_text: Nika’s story No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out. Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of. Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane. Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there. After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east. “They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.” The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her? Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk. cards.source_text: The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns. The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region. The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions. A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden. The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m. External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly. The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment. Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year. At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions. The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency
cards.source_title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns

cards.source_text: WASHINGTON, September 23. /TASS/. The administration of Donald Trump undermined allies’ trust in the United States during negotiations on a deal concerning Greenland, senior Democratic member of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee Jeanne Shaheen (New Hampshire) stated. "After months of threatening our NATO Ally Denmark and disregarding the will of the Greenlandic people, President Trump has reached a 'deal' that essentially returns the US-Greenland defense relationship to where it was before. But President Trump’s threats and bullying rhetoric on this issue have come at a cost: the United States is now viewed with skepticism and increased distrust by some of our closest allies," Shaheen said in a statement on X. According to her, "that has damaged America’s trade relationships and undermined the NATO Alliance." As Shaheen noted, the United States "has real work to do to rebuild trust with Denmark, Greenland and our allies across Europe." Earlier, Trump said that the US and Denmark had reached an agreement on Washington taking control of Greenland’s security. He said that the US would immediately begin to increase its military presence on the Arctic island. The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York by US President Donald Trump, as well as the Prime Ministers of Denmark and Greenland, Mette Frederiksen and Jens·Frederik Nielsen.

cards.source_text: Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” Tuesday as he made his final address to the annual gathering of world leaders convening to face a formidable menu of challenges, from climate change and war to inequality and the rise of artificial intelligence. In a no-nonsense farewell speech, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged global leaders Tuesday to respond to the defining challenge today: Will the world continue on its path to fragmentation, or cooperate to tackle the existential threats from climate crisis, runaway artificial intelligence and intensifying inequalities? Read more'No peace without justice,' Macron tells UN General Assembly The UN leader has long implored leaders not to give up on cooperation and shared decision-making in the face of accelerating global challenges and increasing great-powers competition. Tuesday’s message at the UN General Assembly took on additional urgency because he leaves office at the end of this year. “The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing raging wars, rising temperatures and artificial intelligence, among other matters. Instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections”. His speech opened the main portion of the world's biggest diplomatic meeting of the year. Leaders from the UN's 193 member countries address each other and the international community and air their hopes, plans and grievances. Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognise “that their power isn’t so super”. Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said. Yet about an hour after Guterres spoke, US President Donald Trump offered a different and equally frank view of power. Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly “While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said, touting his country's economic, technological and military footprint. cards.source_text: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting - Published Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday. The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations. The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship". "We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it." Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been". Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI). He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home." The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech. Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros". He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency. His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Torpedo exercise For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history. cards.source_text: WASHINGTON, September 23. /TASS/. The Spanish authorities intend to ban imports of Russian liquefied natural gas from January 1, 2027, despite existing contracts held by Spanish companies for supplies of Russian energy resources, Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said. Speaking at the Atlantic Council in Washington [recognized as an undesirable organization in Russia], he noted that Madrid would comply with the relevant restrictions previously adopted by the European Union. "In fact, these sanctions could not have been introduced without Spain’s consent, as some Spanish companies have existing contracts. As you know, LNG supply contracts are concluded years in advance. These are very long-term contracts. This is not something that can be decided at the last minute, which is why they remain in force for decades. We intend to comply with the requirements of the new sanctions," the minister said. He added that Spain has some of the largest LNG storage and processing capacities. "This also opens up opportunities for the rest of Europe. We can help them with LNG supplies from reliable partners, such as the United States," the Spanish foreign minister said. EU ban on Russian gas On January 26, the EU Council finalized a complete ban on Russian LNG supplies to the EU effective January 1, 2027, and on pipeline gas from September 30, 2027. The ban on LNG imports under short-term contracts came into effect on April 25, 2026, while short-term pipeline gas contracts were set to expire by June 17, 2026. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that, given the EU’s intention to completely phase out Russian gas, Russia could prematurely exit the European market on its own initiative and redirect supplies to other, more interested buyers. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced that Russian companies would soon redirect a portion of LNG supplies from Europe to friendly nations, including China, India, Thailand, and the Philippines, without waiting for further EU restrictions. According to TASS calculations, Russia was the second-largest exporter of LNG to the EU by value in 2025, behind the US. Its share stood at 16.1% (or 16.2% of the combined value of LNG and pipeline gas purchases). In terms of volume, Russia accounted for roughly 14% of the EU’s LNG imports (12.1% of total gas supplies, including pipeline gas). cards.source_text: UNITED NATIONS, September 23. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will lead the Russian delegation beginning his working program on September 23 at the high-level week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, with an address scheduled for September 26. Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova confirmed his schedule is "maximally packed." Russia's position will focus on strengthening multipolarity, building equal and indivisible Eurasian security, countering colonialism, reforming the global financial architecture, combating terrorism, and disarmament. Zakharova said the UN remains "an indispensable and most representative universal platform for multilateral diplomacy." A meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled for Lavrov's first day. He will also meet with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, with over 30 meetings planned with representatives from Algeria, Brazil, India, Iran, Cuba, and others, as well as the OSCE, IAEA, and UN General Assembly President. The upcoming change of UN secretary-general will be a key topic, with Rebeca Grynspan receiving the most support in the latest Security Council straw poll.

cards.source_text: Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers. The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next. Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous. The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely. The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo. Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due to excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy. Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off. cards.source_text: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings - Published Sri Lanka's High Court has given long jail sentences to 15 men charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500. Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted. The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead. All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody. The 15 defendants on Tuesday were each given prison terms ranging from 200 to 260 years. The court in the capital Colombo also ordered the confiscation of their all movable and immovable assets. The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the court in two prison buses. Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children. They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo. The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans. Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there. 'Intelligence lapse' In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. items.title: Viral NATO video falsely framed as ‘war propaganda’ against Russia
items.summary: A viral NATO video is being falsely framed online as “war propaganda”, with users accusing the Alliance of sharing a “promotional video” designed to prepare the public for imminent war with Russia. But the footage is not new: NATO published it in July 2024 for its 75th anniversary, and it’s been stripped of its original context. The claim comes as European leaders warn of growing Russian hybrid threats, including alleged drone, cyber and sabotage activity. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
